summary:
Bremen, as a German city-state, stands under the national framework set by the Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz). It has enacted no trans-specific statute of its own and no prison-placement rule of its own. Prison administration and the civil-registry offices are competences of the city-state, so the layer a trans person actually deals with in Bremen is run by Bremen authorities, applying the federal framework without local amendment.

Under the Self-Determination Act the legal gender entered in the civil registry is the reference point for prison placement in every Land, and § 6(1) SBGG permits Land law to override that entry. Bremen has not passed such an override. The placement of a trans person held in a Bremen facility therefore turns on the registered entry rather than on a Bremen exception clause; how intake review is conducted in Bremen's prisons is not documented in the available sources.

Legal gender changes for Bremen residents are processed through the city-state's own registry offices. Bremen maintains no separate rule on bathrooms, changing or leisure facilities, or identity documents of its own, so a visitor meets the national framework rather than a local variant.
tangentialFactors:
Bremen has no veto over the self-determination framework it applies. A Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, launched by several Länder after the dispute over a prisoner's placement, would take effect in Bremen as federal law if enacted, with no Bremen statute required.

Because registry offices and prison administration are Land competences, the practical handling of a trans person's file or custody in Bremen depends on Bremen authorities rather than on a federal agency, even where the governing rules are federal.
localsOnly:
A trans resident of Bremen changes their legal gender entry at the Bremen registry offices; the procedure follows the federal self-determination rules rather than a Bremen variant.

Prison placement is a Bremen responsibility rather than a federal one, so any change to placement rules in the city-state's own facilities would have to come from Bremen legislation. As it stands, there is no Bremen placement statute to cite, and the registered entry is the governing reference.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bremen-specific enforcement action, court ruling, or incident involving a trans person appears in the sources. The materials document the Bremen position only as an absence of local legislation, so how Bremen's registry offices and prison intake handle individual cases is not sourced.

Placement practice inside Bremen's prisons is not documented in these sources; the question is governed by the federal framework together with the absence of a Bremen exception clause.

No Bremen statistics on trans people in custody, and no Bremen breakdown of discrimination complaints under the General Act on Equal Treatment, are available in the source set.
